whyCorrect: The sentence tells you exactly what the critics did: they were "celebrating" the films and "praising" one as "especially pointed" and the other as "heartbreaking and inspiring." The blank needs a verb that means to speak of something with approval, and that is "commended." When a blank sits between a description of an attitude and quoted evidence of that attitude, the quotes are the definition you are matching.

whyWrong.A: "Inspired" reverses the direction: the critics were affected by the films, not the cause of them. You would need the films to inspire the critics, not the other way around.
whyWrong.B: "Satirized" means mocked, which contradicts "celebrating" and the openly admiring quotes.
whyWrong.C: "Overlooked" means failed to notice, but the critics clearly discussed both films in detail.

tips: Quoted praise inside the sentence is a definition of the blank, not decoration — read it before you look at the choices.

whyCorrect: The second sentence explains the gap: practitioners may reach conclusions based on confounding variables, which means the trial results and the practitioners' conclusions do not line up. So the trials "fail to" confirm what practitioners believe, and "corroborate" means to confirm or support with evidence. The word "fail to" already carries the negative, so the blank itself must be a positive word.

whyWrong.A: "Implement" means to put into practice; trial results do not carry out conclusions, and the point is about agreement, not action.
whyWrong.B: "Disseminate" means to spread widely, which describes publication, not whether the findings match.
whyWrong.C: "Circumvent" means to get around, and "fail to circumvent" would mean the trials did not avoid the conclusions — the opposite of the mismatch being described.

commonMistakes: Students forget that "fail to" flips the polarity and then hunt for a negative word for the blank.

whyCorrect: The colon defines the effect for you: buyers who had not previously wanted the toys "suddenly thronged the market." Demand went up, and it went up because of the price rise, so the blank needs a word meaning "causing or bringing on." "Precipitating" means bringing something about suddenly, which matches both the rise in demand and the word "suddenly."

whyWrong.A: "Exploiting" would mean taking advantage of demand that already existed, but the passage says these buyers had not previously wanted the toys.
whyWrong.B: "Stabilizing" means holding steady, which is not counterintuitive and contradicts the surge described after the colon.
whyWrong.C: "Monetizing" means converting something into revenue; demand is not what gets monetized here, and it does not explain the crowd of new buyers.

tips: After a colon, the rest of the sentence restates the blank — read it first.

whyCorrect: The blank is the subject of "cite the production of less material waste and a faster return on investment" — someone is arguing in favor of modular construction by listing its benefits. "Proponents" means people who advocate for something, and only people can cite advantages. The listed benefits are all positives, so the subject must be supporters rather than neutral parties.

whyWrong.A: "Components" are parts of a thing, not people, and parts cannot cite anything.
whyWrong.B: "Safeguards" are protective measures, which also cannot make an argument.
whyWrong.D: "Epitomes" means perfect examples; an epitome of an approach is a thing, not an advocate, and it cannot cite evidence.

commonMistakes: Choices A and B sound related to construction, which is bait — check whether the blank has to be a person before judging topic fit.

whyCorrect: The end of the sentence says the problem is "unpredictable shifts in cloud cover and haze," so what a storage reserve protects against is collection that keeps going up and down. "Fluctuations in" solar energy collection is exactly that irregular variation. Stored energy is useful precisely because it fills the dips, which only makes sense if collection is inconsistent.

whyWrong.A: "Calibrations with" refers to adjusting instruments; clouds do not calibrate anything, and calibration is not something storage would offset.
whyWrong.B: "Developments of" suggests progress in collection, which is a good thing and would not need mitigating.
whyWrong.D: "Incentives for" refers to encouragements to collect solar energy, which cloud cover does not cause and storage does not counteract.

tips: Match the blank to the cause named at the end of the sentence — "unpredictable shifts" is a synonym clue.

whyCorrect: Almost every sentence is about Max's longing to see La Reina: he has "begged" his father "for as long as he could remember," he imagines being a hero for crossing the gates first, and he hopes "maybe this summer" it will finally happen. A purpose question asks what the whole passage is doing, and here everything points to conveying the strength of that one desire. The ghost detail and his age both work as reasons the wish matters to him, not as separate topics.

whyWrong.B: The father barely appears and his feelings about Max are never described; he is only the person Max is asking.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text criticizes Max, and he looks forward to summer rather than disliking it.
whyWrong.D: "He was almost twelve" signals eagerness to be old enough, not reluctance to grow up.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice built from a detail that appears in the text (the father, summer) instead of the idea the whole passage builds toward.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says copying one feature of a walkable city "may be insufficient" to make another city more walkable. The second sentence explains why: research disagrees about what drives the decision to walk, and real choices depend on many overlapping conditions. Put together, the text is making the case that no single reliable lever for increasing walking has been identified.

whyWrong.B: The text never discusses measuring or comparing pedestrian traffic across cities; San Francisco is only an example of a strategy that may not transfer.
whyWrong.C: Storefront density is mentioned once as an example of a feature that may not transfer, not as the subject of the passage.
whyWrong.D: The text says our understanding of walking decisions is not robust; it offers no proposal for improving how people decide.

tips: When a passage names an example with "e.g." and then generalizes, the general claim is the purpose and the example is support.

whyCorrect: Text 1's claim is that calling Sula "historical fiction" undersells it, because that label suggests "the mere re-creation of the past." Text 2 attacks exactly that assumption, arguing that historical fiction can explore "profound themes and complex characters" and even grants writers extra creative freedom. So Text 2's author would say the objection to the label comes from taking a narrow view of what the genre can do, not from anything about Sula itself.

whyWrong.A: Text 2 explicitly criticizes the idea that historical fiction is about showing off period details, so praising Morrison's period knowledge would undercut its own argument.
whyWrong.C: Text 2 defends the genre as a whole rather than conceding that most of it is unsophisticated.
whyWrong.D: Text 1 already calls Sula "much richer and more complicated," so Text 2 would have no basis for accusing its author of underestimating the novel.

commonMistakes: Reading Text 1 as a criticism of Sula; it praises the novel and criticizes the label.

whyCorrect: The drawback is stated between the dashes: Places API data "tend to be restricted to places that [are] customer facing." That means businesses and amenities the public does not walk into are missing from the data set, so a map built from it cannot cover everything in a neighborhood. Conclusions drawn from an incomplete inventory of amenities are what the limit produces.

whyWrong.A: The text says nothing about the age of the data; the limit is coverage, not timeliness.
whyWrong.B: No claim is made that the method borrows untested advances from other fields.
whyWrong.C: Neighborhood boundaries are not the issue — the model predicts the mix of businesses within a neighborhood.

tips: When a question asks for a drawback, look for the sentence containing a contrast word like "but" or a dash-enclosed aside.

whyCorrect: The second sentence carries the main claim: the Highwaymen's paintings are "remarkable for anticipating and amplifying cultural perceptions of Florida that became pervasive in the public consciousness." "Amplifying" means the paintings helped spread those images, and the recurring iconography — placid rivers, windswept palms — is what became identified with Florida. McLendon's painting is offered only as a typical example of that shared imagery.

whyWrong.A: The text calls Moonlit St. Lucie "typical" of the group's work; it never ranks it above other Highwaymen paintings.
whyWrong.C: Nothing about declining popularity after the 1960s appears; the text says the imagery became pervasive.
whyWrong.D: The rivers and palm trees are shared across the collective, so they cannot distinguish McLendon from his colleagues.

commonMistakes: Treating the opening description of one painting as the main idea when it is only an illustration of the claim in the next sentence.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts, and the quotation has to satisfy both: it must build suspense, and it must do so through the narrator's physical reaction. Choice A does exactly that — an unidentified noise approaches while the narrator lies hidden, and her pounding heart is the physical response she fears will give her away. The danger is unresolved as the quotation ends, which is what makes it suspenseful.

whyWrong.B: Laughter and singing describe a happy scene with no tension and no bodily reaction of the narrator's own.
whyWrong.C: This reports news and travel; it is narrative sequence, not a physical response to an event.
whyWrong.D: This relays what the grandfather told the father — plot information with no suspense and no physical sensation.

commonMistakes: Choosing a quotation that is merely dramatic; the claim names a specific technique, and every part of it has to appear in the quotation.

whyCorrect: The claim is that Aristophanes portrays sophists as having an inflated view of their own wisdom, so you need a sophist praising himself. In choice D, Socrates describes his own teaching as "any clever dogma about abstruse matters" — he calls his own ideas clever and his subject matter profound, in the same breath as instructing the student to be ready to catch them. That self-congratulation is the exaggerated wisdom the claim names.

whyWrong.A: Socrates is insulting the customer here; it shows impatience with someone else, not an inflated estimate of his own wisdom.
whyWrong.B: This is Strepsiades describing what sophists teach and charge for; it mocks their doctrines and greed rather than showing a sophist's self-regard.
whyWrong.C: This quotation is about a music recommendation platform and has nothing to do with The Clouds or sophists.

tips: For a claim about how a character sees himself, the quotation has to come out of that character's own mouth and be about himself.

whyCorrect: The student's claim is that small breeds must share one particular repressing version of the IGF-1 gene. To weaken it you need evidence that small dogs get their small size without all having that same version. Choice D gives exactly that: other small, low-IGF-1 breeds carry a different version of the gene than toy poodles do, so a single shared version cannot be the requirement.

whyWrong.A: Limited activity in the regulating gene among common breeds is consistent with the student's claim rather than against it.
whyWrong.B: Confirming that this gene is the only one with within-breed consistency supports the student's focus on it.
whyWrong.C: How much dogs vary in size compared with other mammals says nothing about which gene version small breeds carry.

commonMistakes: Weakening a claim means contradicting the specific mechanism it asserts, not just adding complication to the topic.

whyCorrect: The key finding is the absence of a plateau: as UVB rises to the highest levels available in mid-latitude zoos, the chimpanzees' vitamin D keeps rising instead of levelling off. A plateau would mean they had hit their biological ceiling; no plateau means more UVB would still have produced more vitamin D. So these chimpanzees are producing less vitamin D than they are capable of producing.

whyWrong.A: The study measured zoo chimpanzees only; nothing compares their levels with wild chimpanzees in the tropics.
whyWrong.B: Correlation with UVB is the ordinary, unadapted response — it is evidence that no new adaptation has appeared.
whyWrong.D: If the chimpanzees are below their capacity, supplementation would be more likely to help, not less.

tips: When a study reports that something does not plateau, the inference is almost always that the ceiling has not been reached.

whyCorrect: The text lines up two things: Liverpool wins at home in mainly red uniforms more often than a non-red team does, and people associate red with dominance and react to it with caution. The conclusion the evidence supports is the cautious, modest one — that opponents facing those red uniforms may have been affected by the color. Notice the hedging in "if applicable" and "may have," which tells you the correct completion will not overstate.

whyWrong.A: Saying opponents were unaffected contradicts the whole point of citing research on reactions to red.
whyWrong.B: The research links red to caution and hesitation, so the predicted effect is less aggression from opponents, not more.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text suggests players were consciously aware of the effect; the research describes an automatic association.

commonMistakes: Reaching for the strongest-sounding conclusion — the correct inference stays inside the hedged language the passage uses.

whyCorrect: Both halves of this sentence are complete on their own: "the exhibition set out to provide a wide-ranging overview...through the 1950s" and "its efforts were largely successful." Two independent clauses cannot simply sit next to each other, and a comma alone cannot join them. A comma plus the coordinating conjunction "and" is a legal join, which is what choice C supplies.

whyWrong.A: With nothing between them the two independent clauses run together as a fused sentence.
whyWrong.B: "And" joining two independent clauses still needs the comma before it.
whyWrong.D: A comma by itself between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

tips: Test each side of the blank as a standalone sentence first; if both stand alone, a bare comma is never enough.

whyCorrect: "The author-as-juggler performs a routine" is a complete sentence, and what follows is a list of three noun phrases — the gathering, the tossing, the catching — that spell out what the routine consists of. A colon is the mark for introducing a list or explanation after a complete clause, so "routine: the" is correct.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, and the list of noun phrases that follows is not a sentence.
whyWrong.B: A comma leaves the three-item list running into the sentence with no signal that it is defining "routine," and it muddles the list's own commas.
whyWrong.C: A period creates a fragment: "The gathering of central themes and tensions, the tossing..., and the catching..." has no verb.

tips: Colon test: complete sentence on the left, and what follows explains or lists what the left side named.

whyCorrect: There are two complete sentences here — "The Great Salt Desert in western Asia is an arid desert" and "it is one of the largest deserts in the world" — so the boundary between them needs a semicolon or a period. The phrase "for example" belongs to the first clause, because the Great Salt Desert is being offered as an example of one of the four desert types just listed. Setting it off with a comma and then closing the clause with a semicolon does both jobs.

whyWrong.B: Two commas leave two independent clauses joined by nothing stronger than a comma — a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: The punctuation is legal, but it attaches "for example" to the second clause, which would make being one of the largest deserts an example of being arid. Size is not an illustration of aridity.
whyWrong.D: With no mark before "it," the two independent clauses fuse into a run-on.

commonMistakes: When two options are both punctuated legally, the decision is about which clause the transition phrase modifies.

whyCorrect: "Having 9,721 feet of prominence" is a modifying phrase, and the noun right after the comma has to be the thing it describes. Only a mountain can have prominence, so the sentence must continue with Pico do Ramelau as its subject. Choice A does that; the rest of its clause then makes the ranking claim.

whyWrong.B: This makes "the list" the subject, so the list is what has 9,721 feet of prominence.
whyWrong.C: This makes "geographers" the subject, so the geographers are the ones with 9,721 feet of prominence.
whyWrong.D: This makes "the ranking" the subject, so the ranking has the prominence — and "is 98th most prominent mountain" is also missing an article.

tips: With an opening -ing phrase, check the first noun after the comma; it must be the doer or the possessor described by that phrase.

whyCorrect: Strip away the opening modifier and you have "Mount Leuser _____ among the world's tallest mountains." The sentence has no other verb, so the blank must supply a finite, conjugated one. "Is ranked" is the only choice that can serve as the main verb.

whyWrong.B: "To rank" is an infinitive and cannot be a sentence's main verb, leaving a fragment.
whyWrong.C: "Ranking" is a participle, which would make the whole thing a long noun phrase with no predicate.
whyWrong.D: "Having ranked" is also a participle, and it would additionally imply the mountain performed the ranking.

commonMistakes: Long introductory phrases hide the fact that the sentence still has no verb — cover the modifier before choosing.

whyCorrect: The second sentence needs a main verb for the plural subject "Puerto Rico museums," and only "inform" is a conjugated verb that agrees with a plural subject. The other options are non-finite forms, so they leave the sentence without a predicate.

whyWrong.B: "Informing" is a participle; "Puerto Rico museums informing visitors about..." is a fragment.
whyWrong.C: "To inform" is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb here.
whyWrong.D: "Having informed" is a participial phrase and also wrongly places the action in a completed past.

tips: If removing the blank leaves a subject with no verb, the answer is the conjugated form.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a claim — the installation is whimsical yet perplexing — and the second sentence confirms it by describing visitors who are "both dazzled and confused." That is the same pair of ideas restated with concrete detail, so you need a transition that intensifies and confirms. "Indeed" does that.

whyWrong.B: "Second" signals the next item in an enumerated list, but no first item was numbered.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" signals a contrast, and the second sentence agrees with the first rather than qualifying it.
whyWrong.D: "Instead" signals a replacement of a rejected alternative, but nothing was rejected.

commonMistakes: Assuming that "whimsical yet perplexing" makes the whole passage contrastive; the contrast is inside the first sentence, and the second sentence supports it.

whyCorrect: The dash clause has already made the contrast — "but this wasn't the case with all elements" — so the next sentence is not opposing anything; it is filling in what happened with those other elements. Niobium, discovered in 1801 and isolated in 1864, is offered as one such case, not as the rule. "Sometimes" marks the sentence as describing that subset of elements.

whyWrong.A: "Moreover" adds a further point of the same kind, but this sentence explains the exception just introduced rather than adding a new one.
whyWrong.B: "Thus" claims the long isolation follows logically from the previous sentence, which merely says not all elements behaved alike.
whyWrong.C: "However" repeats a contrast the word "but" has already made, and no new opposition is being introduced.

tips: If the previous sentence already contains "but," a second contrast word is usually redundant.

whyCorrect: Signing a treaty and ratifying it are two different steps, and the sentence sets them against each other: Colombia did the first but not the second. The phrase "has yet to" marks the second half as falling short of what the first half implies, so the transition must signal contrast. "However" does that.

whyWrong.B: "Similarly" would mean the second clause matches the first, but not ratifying is the opposite of the completed action just described.
whyWrong.C: "Specifically" introduces a narrower restatement, and failing to ratify is not a detail of having signed.
whyWrong.D: "For example" would make the failure to ratify an instance of signing, which it is not.

tips: "Has yet to" almost always signals something withheld or incomplete — expect a contrast transition.

whyCorrect: The goal names two jobs: state a generalization about flag symbols and support it. Choice B states the general claim — some countries put animal symbols on their flags — and then backs it with the raggiana bird-of-paradise on Papua New Guinea's flag. A choice that does only one of the two jobs cannot be right no matter how accurate it is.

whyWrong.A: This gives only the single example, with no general claim for it to illustrate; it also adds "national identity," which the notes do not say.
whyWrong.C: This makes a general statement but supports it with a definition of vexillology rather than with an example of a symbol.
whyWrong.D: This is about the field of study, not about symbols on flags, and it offers no supporting instance.

commonMistakes: Two-part goals are graded on both parts — check for the general claim and the specific evidence separately.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is narrow: name a country whose currency has "dollar" in its name. Choice A names Kiribati and its Kiribati dollar, which is exactly one such example. Anything that does not name a specific country with a dollar-named currency fails the goal even if it is true.

whyWrong.B: This says what Kiribati does not call its currency, which is not an example of using the word "dollar."
whyWrong.C: This gives the etymology of the word, not a country that uses it.
whyWrong.D: This is the general statement the example is supposed to illustrate, with no country named.

tips: Underline the goal sentence and check each choice against it word by word before judging style.

whyCorrect: A generalization has to say something that holds beyond the two specific samples tested. Both seaweeds in the study — macrokelp and ma-konbu — are brown seaweeds and both produced umami ratings, moderate and high, so the claim the notes license is that brown seaweed can trigger umami. Choice D states that as a general property rather than reporting what happened in one study.

whyWrong.A: This just classifies the two seaweeds; it reports category membership, not a general finding.
whyWrong.B: This describes the study's procedure and stops before drawing any conclusion.
whyWrong.C: This also only reports what participants did, and it says "various seaweeds" rather than making a claim about brown seaweed.

commonMistakes: Confusing an accurate summary of the study with a generalization — a generalization must assert something about the category, not about the experiment.

whyCorrect: The "shortcoming" is the narrow focus on a few countries, caused by limited data. The second sentence says researchers gained access to banking records in Africa and Eastern Europe, which broadens the data and therefore reduces the problem. "Mitigate" means to make less severe, which is what wider data does to a narrowness caused by missing data.

whyWrong.B: "Validate" means to confirm as legitimate, but new data corrects the flaw rather than endorsing it.
whyWrong.C: "Presuppose" means to assume in advance, and researchers cannot assume in advance a limitation they are working to fix afterward.
whyWrong.D: "Categorize" means to sort into groups, which does nothing to the shortcoming and is not what expanded access accomplishes.

tips: When a sentence names a problem and then reports something that fixes its cause, the blank is a verb meaning "reduce."

whyCorrect: The colon spells out the meaning: "many of the companies could not operate if they had to do everything necessary to find investors for themselves." So without the service, the time and expense would be so high that the companies could not function. "Prohibitive" means costly enough to prevent something, which is precisely that.

whyWrong.A: "Misconstrued" means misunderstood, but the issue is the size of the cost, not anyone's interpretation of it.
whyWrong.B: "Distinctive" means notably different, which says nothing about whether the companies could bear the cost.
whyWrong.D: "Beneficial" reverses the meaning — the cost is what the service saves companies from, not something good for them.

commonMistakes: Skipping the clause after the colon; it defines the blank.

whyCorrect: The mosque is described as one of the largest in the world, holding around 24,000 people, and the sentence begins "Few religious buildings can be said to ____ the astonishing size" of it. If very few buildings can do this, the verb has to be one that only an equally huge building could perform — that is, equal it. "Match" fits.

whyWrong.A: "Conceal" would mean hiding the mosque's size, which no other building does or could.
whyWrong.B: "Symbolize" would mean standing for its size, which makes no sense as something buildings compete to do.
whyWrong.C: "Minimize" would mean making its size seem smaller, and there is nothing in the sentence about downplaying it.

tips: "Few X can be said to ___" is a superlative frame: the blank is nearly always a verb meaning equal, rival, or surpass.

whyCorrect: After the colon the sentence tells you what happened: buyers who had not previously wanted the figures "thronged the market." Demand did not just shift, it came into existence where there had been none, so the blank needs a verb meaning to bring about or produce. "Engendering" means giving rise to, which matches new demand created by the price rise.

whyWrong.A: "Monetizing" means turning something into a source of revenue; demand is what drives revenue, not what gets converted into it.
whyWrong.B: "Appraising" means assessing value, which is something people do to the toys, not an effect a price rise has on demand.
whyWrong.D: "Exploiting" means taking advantage of demand that already exists, but the passage specifies buyers who had not previously wanted these toys.

tips: "Counterintuitive effect of ___ demand" tells you the price rise caused something surprising to happen to demand — the blank is a cause verb.

whyCorrect: The second sentence defines the blank: "Only material objects—such as the fossil remains...—can show whether a particular idea about the Pliocene is defensible." Material objects are physical things, so the evidence paleontologists must turn to is physical evidence. The word "only" tells you the blank names the sole acceptable kind, not a desirable extra quality.

whyWrong.B: "Convenient" describes ease of access, and fossils dug up in Ethiopia are not being praised for convenience.
whyWrong.C: "Creative" describes imaginative thinking, which is the opposite of what "only material objects" allows.
whyWrong.D: "Inconclusive" would mean the evidence settles nothing, contradicting the claim that it can show whether an idea is defensible.

commonMistakes: Looking only at the sentence with the blank; here the definition sits entirely in the next sentence.

whyCorrect: Track the text in three moves. It reports a finding (moonlight suppresses pocket mouse activity) and immediately explains it in cost-benefit terms; then it says most other nocturnal mammals behave the same way, making the finding representative; then it names night monkeys as an exception and explains that exception by their reliance on visual foraging. Choice B is the only option that keeps the exception explained rather than left open or treated as a problem.

whyWrong.A: The night monkey exception does not cast doubt on the cost-benefit explanation — it is accounted for by that same cost-benefit logic applied to a visual forager.
whyWrong.C: Both responses are explained, so it is wrong to say the second still needs explaining.
whyWrong.D: The difference for night monkeys is attributed to their foraging biology, not to any difference in study methods.

tips: Structure questions turn on the last clause as often as the first — check whether the exception is explained, doubted, or left hanging.

whyCorrect: Sentence one defines community science as a research approach. Sentence two lists what it can do — support conservation, spark youth interest, increase data collected. Sentence three names one study, on butterfly color and flower choice, that used the approach. That is: approach, benefits, example, which is choice B.

whyWrong.A: The text never gives the study's results; it only says the approach was essential to the study's success.
whyWrong.C: No public opinion is mentioned, and the text presents community science as already established rather than arguing for something new.
whyWrong.D: Nothing traces how the collaboration developed over time, and no future projects are proposed.

commonMistakes: Choosing a structure that sounds like it fits when one of its three parts (results, public opinion, future work) never appears in the passage.

whyCorrect: The relevant sentence says friction between pieces of graphene is "generally extremely low," and that when the researchers added a drop of oil "that friction nearly vanished." So the starting point was already very low friction, and the oil pushed it lower still. Choice B states exactly that two-step change.

whyWrong.A: Nothing is said about graphene migrating to one surface; the fragments were applied to cover both.
whyWrong.C: The nanotubes were broken into graphene fragments before the coating was applied, and the oil is not described as breaking anything.
whyWrong.D: The text says friction nearly vanished, so it changed dramatically rather than not noticeably.

tips: A detail question is answered by one sentence — find it and paraphrase it rather than reasoning from the passage's general topic.

whyCorrect: The second sentence says Hooks and Ward "had met while performing in a 1960 touring production of Lorraine Hansberry's play A Raisin in the Sun." Performing in a production means acting in it, so their first meeting was as fellow actors in that show. Everything else in the passage happens after 1967, which is later than their meeting.

whyWrong.A: NEC's workshops came after 1967, years after the two men had already met and cofounded the company.
whyWrong.B: Harrison is mentioned only as a playwright whose work NEC produced in 1974; he does not introduce anyone.
whyWrong.C: The Great MacDaddy was produced in 1974, long after the 1960 meeting, and they performed rather than attended.

commonMistakes: Grabbing the most prominent play in the passage instead of the one attached to the date of the meeting.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts Władysław I Herman, whose reign is given precise dates from 1079 to 1102, with Lestek, who "is said to have ruled" but "whose historical actuality is disputed." "Historical actuality is disputed" means historians argue about whether he existed at all, while Herman's existence is not in question. The oral-tradition detail at the end explains why the record for Lestek is weaker.

whyWrong.A: The chronicle's account of Lestek is described as weaker evidence, since it rests on oral tradition unlike its records of later rulers.
whyWrong.C: Lestek is placed in the 9th and 10th centuries, earlier than Herman's 1079-1102 rule, not later.
whyWrong.D: It is Lestek, not Herman, whose record depends on orally transmitted material, and the passage treats that as a reason for doubt.

tips: "Historical actuality is disputed" is formal phrasing for "we are not sure this person existed" — translate it before scanning the choices.

whyCorrect: The claim has a cause and an effect: putting on particular clothes changes how Mrs. Sommers sees herself. Choice D names the clothes — stockings, boots, gloves — and then states the inner change directly: they "had given her a feeling of assurance, a sense of belonging to the well-dressed multitude." That is a shift in her sense of self attributed to the garments, which is exactly the claim.

whyWrong.A: This describes her habits as a bargain hunter, an established trait rather than a change caused by wearing something.
whyWrong.B: She looks at her new boots here, but the quotation reports only her posture and glance, not any change in how she regards herself.
whyWrong.C: This is her plan to buy fabric for her children; no clothing is worn and no self-perception is mentioned.

tips: When a claim names a cause and an effect, the quotation must contain both — clothing alone is not enough.

whyCorrect: The writer's claim is comparative: Thomas's work improved when she left figurative art for abstraction. Support therefore has to put the two modes side by side and rate them differently. Choice C does that, calling the realistic 1964 still life "labored" while the abstract 1970 Lunar Surface "glows with rich splashes of purple and blue."

whyWrong.A: This describes color in one abstract painting but offers no figurative work to compare it against, so it cannot show a change for the better.
whyWrong.B: Her interest in nature spans both phases of her career and says nothing about abstraction versus figuration.
whyWrong.D: This is about her beliefs regarding what art can depict, not about the quality of her figurative versus abstract work.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that praises the abstract work alone — a claim about a turning point needs evidence from both sides of the turn.

whyCorrect: The student claims The Horse Fair marks a significant change in Bonheur's development, so the supporting quotation has to show a before-and-after break in her work. Choice A does: the paintings before it belong to an earlier style "to which she never returned." That establishes the painting as the dividing line between two phases.

whyWrong.B: Calling it her most representative work makes it a summary of her abilities, not a turning point in them.
whyWrong.C: Disagreement about the painting's meaning speaks to interpretation, not to any change in her development.
whyWrong.D: Being ahead of her time compares Bonheur with other artists rather than with her own earlier work.

tips: "Marks a change" claims need evidence about what came before and after, not evidence about quality or reputation.

whyCorrect: Follow the chain: the songs describe terraced clam gardens, and archaeological evidence shows that where the practice was common, clams grew larger and more abundant despite heavier harvesting. So the songs record a technique that actually worked for growing a food source. The completion has to state that generalization — cultivation methods for food are part of what Indigenous songs preserve.

whyWrong.A: "Defining characteristic" of the music is far too strong; the passage says ecological information can be transmitted in songs, not that it defines them.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the reasoning into a claim about why the songs were made, which the evidence about clam size cannot establish.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the passage compares the species of clams then and now.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that sounds most specific; the phrase "demonstrates that" calls for the conclusion the evidence actually licenses.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up two facts: longitudinal sampling over many years demands extensive financial support, and a study that only counts daily riders has no need of longitudinal methods. Put together, the transportation study can be done without the expensive method, so it should cost far less. The word "and so" signals that the completion is the consequence of those two facts.

whyWrong.A: This compares SOEP with a longitudinal transportation study, but the point is that the transportation study need not be longitudinal at all.
whyWrong.B: Authority of conclusions is not at issue; each method suits its own question.
whyWrong.C: The passage says longitudinal methods are unnecessary when causation is irrelevant, which is narrower than a blanket rule that transportation studies should avoid them.

tips: When the completion follows "and so," combine the two premises the passage just gave rather than adding a new judgment.

whyCorrect: "Little-known French portrait artist" is a title-like description attached directly to the name that follows, the same structure as "painter Villers." A name used this way is restrictive — it identifies which artist — so no punctuation separates the description from the name. Choice B leaves the phrase unbroken.

whyWrong.A: A dash creates a sharp break where the description and the name form a single unit.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete clause, and "was actually the work of little-known French portrait artist" is not one.
whyWrong.D: A comma would make the name a nonrestrictive aside, wrongly implying the description already identifies a single known person.

tips: Title plus name — "the artist Villers," "the novelist Morrison" — takes no punctuation between them.

whyCorrect: The pronoun stands in for what received skepticism: Duchamp's "abstract cubist aesthetic," a singular noun. A singular thing takes the singular pronoun "it." Read the clause on its own — "as it represented a radical departure" — and the agreement is obvious.

whyWrong.A: "These" is plural and has no plural noun to refer back to.
whyWrong.B: "They" is also plural; the artists named earlier are not what the clause is explaining.
whyWrong.C: "We" introduces a first person that appears nowhere in the passage.

commonMistakes: Letting the nearby plural "critics" or "artists" drag you into a plural pronoun — the pronoun must match the thing that did the departing.

whyCorrect: The subject of the verb is "analysis," which is singular; "of de jure judicial independence and its growth over decades" is a prepositional phrase, and a noun inside a prepositional phrase can never be the subject. Cut that phrase and you are left with "analysis _____ six constitutional features," which takes the singular "identifies." The scholars' names sit inside a possessive, so they cannot control the verb either.

whyWrong.A: "Have identified" is plural, agreeing with the two scholars rather than with "analysis."
whyWrong.C: "Are identifying" is plural and also puts a finished study into ongoing present progressive.
whyWrong.D: "Identify" is the plural present form and does not agree with the singular subject.

commonMistakes: Letting a plural possessive ("Melton and Ginsburg's") or a plural object of a preposition set the verb number.

whyCorrect: Find the subject by stripping the modifiers: "the 66-kilometer-per-second collision between these meteoroids and atmospheric gases" reduces to "the collision," which is singular. A singular subject in the present takes "produces." The plural nouns "meteoroids" and "gases" sit inside the phrase "between...," so neither governs the verb.

whyWrong.B: "Are producing" is plural and shifts to a progressive that clashes with the recurring, every-year framing.
whyWrong.C: "Produce" is the plural form, agreeing with "meteoroids" instead of "collision."
whyWrong.D: "Have produced" is plural and places the event in the past-through-present rather than describing what happens each year.

tips: Cross out every "of" and "between" phrase before choosing the verb — the subject is what remains.

whyCorrect: "The cellular organs that generate energy from light" is a definition inserted into the sentence, and it already ends with a dash before "reshuffled." Punctuation around an interrupting element has to match at both ends, so the opening mark must also be a dash. Choice B supplies it.

whyWrong.A: A comma to open and a dash to close is a mismatched pair.
whyWrong.C: With no opening mark the definition runs straight into the subject, leaving the closing dash unpaired.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, and neither piece here is one.

tips: When one end of an interrupter is already punctuated in the passage, your only job is to match it.

whyCorrect: What follows is a list of three items, each already containing a comma, which is why the items are separated by semicolons: "at 296 light-years away, the gas giant 42 Draconis b; and...over 1,000 other exoplanets." The first item has to match that pattern — "at 204 light-years away, the Neptune-like planet DMPP-1 b" — and the whole list has to be introduced. A colon after the complete clause ending in "Earth" does the introducing.

whyWrong.A: Without a colon the list is never introduced, and the commas around the distance phrase make it read as a description of Earth.
whyWrong.B: This has neither the colon nor the comma structure the parallel items require.
whyWrong.C: Putting the colon after "away" attaches the distance to Earth and breaks parallelism with the later items, which each begin with their distance phrase.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the items further down the list — they show you the pattern the first item must copy.

whyCorrect: The first sentence ends with a claim: the upward trend in urbanization appeared throughout South Asia. The second sentence backs that claim with the regional figures, 34.5% rising to 36.6% over the same years. A transition that confirms and reinforces a claim just made is "Indeed."

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" signals contrast, but the regional numbers agree with the claim rather than qualifying it.
whyWrong.C: "In reality" signals a correction of something mistaken, and nothing in the first sentence is being corrected.
whyWrong.D: "Later" signals a subsequent time period, but both sentences cover the identical span from 2015 to 2020.

tips: When the second sentence gives numbers that prove the first, look for a confirming transition, not a contrasting one.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a cause — Kelley did extensive research for the book — and the second gives the result — colleagues treated it as reliable. Reliability follows from the research, so the transition has to signal effect. "Consequently" does.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" signals a parallel case, but the two sentences are one cause and its outcome, not two similar things.
whyWrong.C: "Next" signals sequence alone and drops the causal link the sentences clearly have.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" signals a surprise, but a well-researched book being judged reliable is the expected result.

commonMistakes: Settling for a sequence word when the sentences are actually related by cause and effect.

whyCorrect: The two sentences have the same shape: one species inherits specific physical traits from its parents, and so does another. Neither causes the other and neither restates the other in different words; they are parallel examples of one principle. "Similarly" is the transition for that relationship.

whyWrong.A: "In other words" would mean the second sentence rephrases the first, but it introduces a different species and different traits.
whyWrong.B: "As a result" would make cat inheritance a consequence of human inheritance, which is not a causal chain.
whyWrong.C: "In conclusion" signals a final summary, and the second sentence adds a new example instead of wrapping up.

tips: Two sentences with matching structure and different subjects almost always call for a comparison transition.

whyCorrect: The goal is to give an example of a poem from Morning Haiku, so the sentence must name a poem and tie it to that book. Choice A does both: it identifies the poem and places it in Sanchez's 2010 collection, then adds its form. A sentence that names only the book, or only the poem without its source, does not present it as an example from the collection.

whyWrong.B: This explains Sanchez's reason for choosing the haiku form and names no poem at all.
whyWrong.C: This describes the book as a whole, so it gives the container rather than an example from it.
whyWrong.D: This describes the poem's form but never names it or connects it to Morning Haiku, so nothing marks it as an example from that book.

tips: For "provide an example of X from Y" goals, check that both X and Y actually appear in the sentence.

whyCorrect: The notes build one chain: Bread is a linocut, lino cutting is a kind of relief printing, and relief printing means carving an image into a block. Choice B is the only option that links Catlett's actual practice to both the named technique and what the technique involves — she used lino cutting, a relief method, carving into linoleum tile. The other choices give a piece of the chain without connecting it to her work.

whyWrong.A: This is a general fact about relief printing materials and never mentions Catlett or her print.
whyWrong.C: This connects Catlett to relief printing but drops the specific technique, lino cutting, that the notes single out.
whyWrong.D: This defines the general process with no reference to Catlett, so it does not describe what she did.

commonMistakes: Choosing a true statement from the notes that leaves out the artist the goal is about.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow — say whom the award is named for. Only choice C answers that: the award honors British mathematician Alan Turing. Correct information about winners or criteria does not satisfy a goal about the award's namesake.

whyWrong.A: This describes a recipient and his achievement, not the person the award is named after.
whyWrong.B: This gives the criteria for the award rather than its namesake.
whyWrong.D: This states when Reddy won and answers nothing about the name.

tips: Rhetorical synthesis goals are graded literally — if the goal says "whom," the answer must name a person and say the award carries that name.

whyCorrect: The second sentence gives the evidence: critics called one film "electrifying" and the other "picture-perfect." Both are strong praise, so the blank describes how the films are now regarded — with approval. "Favorably" is the adverb for that. The opening "Whatever the general attitude...when they were initially released" sets up a contrast with the past, which tells you the present view is decidedly positive rather than mixed.

whyWrong.A: "Strangely" describes an odd manner of regard, which the quoted praise does not show.
whyWrong.B: "Neutrally" means without strong feeling, contradicting two enthusiastic superlatives.
whyWrong.C: "Skeptically" means with doubt, the opposite of the critics' praise.

tips: Quoted critical language after "for example" is the definition of the blank.

whyCorrect: The second sentence calls the portraits "characteristic works" and "esteemed," so Edwards is known and admired for doing this. A "reputation for" painting portraits captures being widely known for that work. The blank needs a noun that a person can have and that fits with the praise in the next sentence.

whyWrong.A: A "complaint about" painting portraits would mean he objects to the work he is celebrated for.
whyWrong.B: A "question about" the portraits would signal doubt, which the word "esteemed" rules out.
whyWrong.C: A "requirement for" painting portraits would mean something is demanded of him, not that he is known for it.

commonMistakes: Choosing a grammatically smooth phrase without checking whether the next sentence is positive or negative.

whyCorrect: The semicolon means the second half defines the first: the delta is "a constantly evolving network of channels and strips of land that change in size and shape." A word meaning constantly changing is "dynamic." The blank is not asking for a judgment about the delta, only a one-word summary of the description that follows.

whyWrong.B: "Immutable" means unchanging, the direct opposite of "constantly evolving."
whyWrong.C: "Sustainable" concerns whether something can be maintained over time, which the description of shifting sediment does not address.
whyWrong.D: "Unrivaled" means unmatched, but the sentence opens with "As with other river deltas," placing it among similar systems rather than above them.

tips: After a semicolon that restates, pick the word that means the same as the restatement — not the word that sounds most impressive.

whyCorrect: The dash clause tells you the intended meaning: "other economists clearly find her studies valuable for their own scholarship." Frequent citation is therefore evidence for the usefulness of her research, so the blank must be a verb meaning to emphasize or confirm. "Underscores" is that verb.

whyWrong.A: "Forestalls" means prevents in advance, which citation does not do to usefulness.
whyWrong.B: "Belies" means contradicts or gives a false impression of, reversing the relationship the dash clause states.
whyWrong.D: "Overshadows" means makes something seem less important, again the opposite of the confirmation described.

commonMistakes: Confusing "belies" with "reveals" — it means the evidence misrepresents, not that it demonstrates.

whyCorrect: The sentence is built on a contrast marked by "though": one body of research is set against below-sea-level studies, which have received "comparatively little notice." The word "comparatively" tells you the first kind of study must be plentiful, since that is what the second is being measured against. "Abundant" supplies that contrast.

whyWrong.B: "Equivocal" means ambiguous in meaning, which describes findings' clarity, not how much research exists.
whyWrong.C: "Sporadic" means occasional, which would match rather than contrast with "little notice."
whyWrong.D: "Preliminary" means early-stage, again describing the research's maturity rather than its quantity.

tips: "Comparatively little" on one side of a contrast forces "a lot" on the other side.

whyCorrect: The passage opens with a long-standing hypothesis — mammoths were hunted to extinction with Clovis-point spears — then spends the rest of its length on one experiment: spears launched into clay, penetrating only a few inches, too shallow to have killed a mammoth. It closes with the conclusion that Clovis hunters likely were not the main cause. That is a description of an experiment used to undercut an accepted idea.

whyWrong.A: No ongoing debate is described; there is one long-held hypothesis and one test of it.
whyWrong.B: The clay-mound method is described but never evaluated for strengths or weaknesses.
whyWrong.C: Only one hypothesis is presented; the anthropologist's conclusion is a result, not a rival hypothesis with its own finding.

commonMistakes: Reading the closing conclusion as a second hypothesis; it is what the experiment showed about the first one.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences establish something true of all baleen whales: they filter krill through baleen plates and can eat up to 30 percent of their mass per day. The rest of the passage then contrasts the humpback with the much heavier northern right whale, which consumes as much as 24,000 kg of krill daily. Because the feeding amount scales with mass, the size difference is a difference within the shared characteristic, which is what choice A says.

whyWrong.B: Baleen feeding is shared by all baleen whales, not unique to humpbacks, and the right whale is not said to lack anything.
whyWrong.C: The order is reversed: the shared feature comes first and the size contrast second.
whyWrong.D: No change in whale populations and no unexpected consequence appear anywhere in the text.

tips: For structure questions, note the order in which ideas appear — a choice with the right pieces in the wrong sequence is still wrong.

whyCorrect: Text 1's whole argument stays inside the question of poetic form: experimental form gets too much scholarly attention and conventional form too little. Text 2 says that scholars' preoccupation with "experimental versus conventional poetic forms" has been "inhibiting inquiry into other points of stylistic correspondence." So Text 2's author would treat Text 1's emphasis as an instance of exactly that obstacle — it keeps other stylistic dimensions out of view.

whyWrong.B: Text 2 never discusses how form affects readers; its complaint is about what scholars study.
whyWrong.C: Text 2 says distant reading can reveal overlooked shared features, not that it has refuted a misconception about modernist poetry.
whyWrong.D: Text 2 casts the form debate as blocking other stylistic study rather than complementing it.

commonMistakes: Assuming Text 2 must reject Text 1's specific claims; it objects to the category of question Text 1 is asking.

whyCorrect: The findings sentence reports two things: color might influence behavior more than size does, and butterflies fed most often in the morning. A main-idea statement has to cover both, at the same strength the passage uses — "might" and "seem to," not certainty. Choice D captures color and time of day as possible influences on behavior.

whyWrong.A: Study location is never measured or mentioned as a factor.
whyWrong.B: The passage compares color with size, not with time of day, and never ranks color below time of day.
whyWrong.C: The community science method is background detail; the text draws no conclusion about when such collaboration is most useful.

tips: Match the hedging: if the passage says "might," a choice that asserts a firm ranking is overstating it.

whyCorrect: The last sentence gives both numbers directly: 30 percent of field mustard seeds sprouted in simulated Martian soil, compared with 4 percent in Earth soil. The question asks for the Martian figure, so it is 30 percent. The trap is grabbing whichever number is nearer the words "field mustard" instead of tracking which soil each figure belongs to.

whyWrong.A: 18 percent appears nowhere in the passage.
whyWrong.C: 100 percent would mean every seed sprouted, which the passage does not claim for any species.
whyWrong.D: 5 percent is a near-miss for the 4 percent Earth-soil figure, and it is the wrong soil in any case.

tips: On a two-number comparison, underline which condition each number belongs to before looking at the choices.

whyCorrect: The conclusion has two parts that must both be supported: prevalence of the deceptive display tracks absolute latitude of brooding sites, and it does so independent of avian order. Choice D reports prevalence across the orders in the study rising from about 34% at 0°-30° to about 60% at 50°-80°, so latitude predicts the trait when orders are pooled rather than separated. That is the pattern the conclusion describes.

whyWrong.A: This compares where species generally brood with where display-using birds brood, which mixes two different populations and gives no per-latitude prevalence rate.
whyWrong.B: This makes Charadriiformes behave differently from other orders, which contradicts the "independent of avian order" part of the conclusion.
whyWrong.C: This also singles out Charadriiformes as unaffected by latitude, again undercutting the claim that order does not matter.

commonMistakes: Supporting only the latitude half of the conclusion and ignoring the "independent of order" half — a choice that makes one order an exception weakens rather than supports.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis predicts a head-to-head difference: in low visibility, intermediate-headed fish detect large-vortex obstructions better than wide-headed fish do. Support therefore needs both head types tested under those conditions, with the intermediate-headed fish doing better. Choice B gives exactly that — the wide-headed species collided with obstructions more often than the intermediate-headed one, which is what worse detection looks like.

whyWrong.A: Equal collision rates show no difference between head shapes, which contradicts the prediction rather than supporting it.
whyWrong.C: Variation among individuals of a single species says nothing about how head shape compares across species.
whyWrong.D: A collision rate for the wide-headed species alone has no intermediate-headed comparison, so it cannot show which detects better.

tips: A comparative hypothesis needs comparative evidence — one group's result on its own can never support it.

whyCorrect: First fix the scale: a low IWCI score means low community integrity, so worse for waterbirds. The hypothesis says hardening harms waterbirds more than development does, which requires a site pair where the two factors point in opposite directions. Choice A supplies it — Back River is heavily developed but barely hardened and scores higher, while Margothy is less developed but more hardened and scores lower, so the hardening is tracking the harm.

whyWrong.B: This is the same setup with the scores reversed, so it shows development doing more damage than hardening.
whyWrong.C: Comparing how similar scores are within pairs measures variability, not which factor is more harmful.
whyWrong.D: Here both development and hardening are high at one site and low at the other, so the two factors cannot be told apart.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that low IWCI means worse; every comparison flips if you read the scale backwards.

whyCorrect: The passage sets a traditional belief — these cities sat on "extremely dry" riverbanks — against Pournelle's evidence that the ground was marshy wetland. Marshland is wet, so the finding directly contradicts the dryness assumption. The completion has to state that contradiction and nothing more, because the passage gives no other evidence to build on.

whyWrong.A: No dates are given, so nothing in the finding bears on which city was founded first.
whyWrong.B: Fish species are never mentioned, and modern river ecology is outside the passage entirely.
whyWrong.D: Trade is not discussed; wetlands say nothing about commercial contact between regions.

tips: When a finding directly contradicts a stated belief, the correct completion is usually the plain restatement of that contradiction, not a further speculation.

whyCorrect: The passage builds one contrast. Massey's abstraction follows Abstract Expressionism so closely that "few viewers would infer...that Massey was Indigenous." Earles instead builds his abstract compositions from motifs drawn from Caddo ceramics and graphic art, so the tribal source stays visible in the finished work. The effect of his abstraction is therefore the opposite of the effect in Untitled: Indigenous identity is easier to see, not harder.

whyWrong.B: The motifs are Caddo in origin and not claimed by Abstract Expressionism, so there is nothing to reclaim.
whyWrong.C: The passage describes Earles working with his own tribal sources, not confronting the demographics of Abstract Expressionism.
whyWrong.D: Untitled is described as aligned with Abstract Expressionism rather than as a site of uneasy coexistence needing reconciliation.

commonMistakes: Treating "in contrast" as an invitation to pick the most political-sounding option instead of the exact reversal of what was just said.

whyCorrect: "The US Geological Survey compiles such data in several ways" is a complete sentence, and what follows is a three-part list of those ways: by exchanging information, by linking maps, and by maintaining a database. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces such a list, and the list itself begins with lowercase "by."

whyWrong.A: A period makes the list a fragment — "By exchanging information..., by linking..., and by maintaining..." has no subject or main verb.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon also demands an independent clause after it, and the list of "by" phrases is not one.
whyWrong.D: "Ways by:" strands the preposition before the colon and breaks the parallel "by" that each list item needs.

tips: Colon before a list, and only when the words before the colon could stand alone as a sentence.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand alone: "the Longyearbyen observatory site monitors activity in the upper atmosphere of the northern hemisphere" and "in Australia, another observatory site, Buckland Park, monitors the sky of the southern hemisphere." Two independent clauses need a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. Only the semicolon is available here.

whyWrong.A: "And" joining two independent clauses still requires a comma before it, and none is offered.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

tips: The second clause already carries internal commas, which is another reason the boundary mark has to be stronger than a comma.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its main verb, "had to devise," so the blank cannot supply another one. What is needed is a modifier describing the chemical reactions — the ones that happen within molecules in a quadrillionth of a second — and a present participle does that job. "Occurring" attaches cleanly to "chemical reactions."

whyWrong.A: "Occurred" is a finite past-tense verb, which would create a second main verb with no conjunction joining it.
whyWrong.C: "Occur" is also finite and leaves the clause ungrammatical after the comma.
whyWrong.D: "Will occur" is finite and puts these reactions in the future, contradicting the description of what Zewail measured.

tips: If the sentence already has a working main verb, a describing phrase needs an -ing or -ed participle, not another conjugated verb.

whyCorrect: Two things have to be right here. The title follows the noun phrase "oil painting" and identifies which painting is meant, so it is restrictive and takes no comma before it. The "which" clause that follows adds extra information about a painting already identified by name, so it is nonrestrictive and does need a comma in front of it. Choice C is the only option with no comma before the title and one before "which."

whyWrong.A: This omits the comma before "which," turning added information into a restrictive clause and running the sentence together.
whyWrong.B: Commas on both sides make the title a removable aside, but without it "oil painting" does not identify which work is meant.
whyWrong.D: This puts the comma in the wrong place entirely — before the title instead of before "which."

tips: A "which" clause giving extra detail always takes a comma; a title that tells you which one takes none.

whyCorrect: Remove the long appositive between the commas and the sentence reads "Oscar James Dunn _____ his term as lieutenant governor in 1868." There is no other verb anywhere, so the blank must be a finite past-tense verb. "Began" is the only choice that qualifies.

whyWrong.A: "To begin" is an infinitive and cannot serve as a main verb, leaving a fragment.
whyWrong.B: "Having begun" is a participial phrase, so the sentence still has no predicate.
whyWrong.C: "Beginning" is a participle and turns the whole string into a long noun phrase.

commonMistakes: A long interrupting phrase makes the sentence feel finished — cover it up and check whether a verb is actually there.

whyCorrect: This is a three-item list matching the three directors named earlier: Zoot Suit (1981), El Norte (1983), and Stand and Deliver (1988). Items in a series are separated by commas, including one before the closing "and" that the passage already supplies. Choice D provides both commas the series needs.

whyWrong.A: This leaves out the comma after "(1981)," so the first two titles run together.
whyWrong.B: With no commas at all the three titles are not separated as list items.
whyWrong.C: Dashes set off an interruption, but El Norte is a member of the list, not an aside.

tips: Count the items before you punctuate — three parallel items take commas, not dashes.

whyCorrect: The sentence with the blank concedes something awkward for the opening claim: this architecture, for all its botanical glasswork, "could not exactly grow in a forest." The next sentence starts with "Still," and returns to the natural influences, which is the classic concession-then-rebuttal pattern. The blank therefore needs a concession marker, and "Of course" is one.

whyWrong.B: "Similarly" claims the sentence matches the first, but it is granting a limitation instead.
whyWrong.C: "Furthermore" adds more evidence for the first claim, and this sentence pulls the other way.
whyWrong.D: "Thus" would make the limitation a consequence of championing nature, which is not the logic.

tips: If the following sentence begins with "Still" or "Nevertheless," the sentence before it is almost always a concession.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a general rule: sleek vehicles are more aerodynamic than bulky ones. The second sentence names a specific sleek vehicle, the F-4 Phantom II, and a specific bulky one, a semitruck, and reports exactly the behavior the rule predicts. That is illustration, so "for example" is the transition.

whyWrong.A: "However" signals contrast, but the jet and the truck confirm the rule rather than complicating it.
whyWrong.B: "Meanwhile" signals a simultaneous or unrelated situation, not an instance of a stated principle.
whyWrong.D: "Additionally" would introduce a new separate point, and this sentence is the same point made concrete.

commonMistakes: Seeing the "while a boxy semitruck" contrast inside the sentence and choosing a contrast transition for the sentence itself.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives Greenidge-Sabral's motivation — she wanted to avoid harsh synthetic dyes — and the second gives what she did about it: experimenting with natural dyes from plants. The action follows from the goal, so the transition should carry that motivation forward. "With this in mind" does exactly that.

whyWrong.B: "To sum up" signals a closing summary, but the second sentence introduces new specifics rather than recapping.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" signals that the action goes against the stated wish, when it in fact fulfills it.
whyWrong.D: "In actuality" signals a correction of a mistaken impression, and nothing in the first sentence is being corrected.

tips: Goal in sentence one plus action in sentence two calls for a purpose or result transition.

whyCorrect: To refute the claim that apricots beat kale you must put both numbers side by side and state the comparison. Choice D does that: 120 mg per 100 g for kale against 10 mg per 100 g for apricots, with the explicit conclusion that kale is the better source. A sentence that gives only kale's figure leaves the reader to do the refuting.

whyWrong.A: This reports kale's content accurately but never mentions apricots, so it does not contradict the claim.
whyWrong.B: Saying both foods contain vitamin C supports neither side of the comparison.
whyWrong.C: This explains why humans need dietary vitamin C and treats the two foods as equivalent sources.

tips: "Refute" goals require the opposing claim to be addressed directly, which usually means both sides of the comparison appear in the sentence.

whyCorrect: Refuting the claim requires the comparison to be made explicitly, with the numbers that decide it. Choice C sets 80 mg per 100 g of brussels sprouts against 13 mg per 100 g of cranberries and states the conclusion that brussels sprouts are the better source. Nothing weaker than a direct comparison can overturn a comparative claim.

whyWrong.A: Noting that both foods contain vitamin C leaves the two equal and refutes nothing.
whyWrong.B: This gives only the brussels sprouts figure, so the reader has no cranberry number to weigh it against.
whyWrong.D: This explains why dietary vitamin C matters and treats the two foods as interchangeable sources.

commonMistakes: Choosing a true, relevant sentence that stops short of the comparison the goal demands.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize a difference, so the sentence has to mention both birds and set one against the other. Choice C names both and contrasts them on size, with "Though they share several traits in common" making the contrast explicit. A sentence describing one bird alone cannot emphasize a difference no matter how detailed it is.

whyWrong.A: This groups the two birds together as members of the same set, which stresses similarity rather than difference.
whyWrong.B: This describes only the sooty-capped hermit, so there is no comparison.
whyWrong.D: This describes only the fiery-tailed awlbill, again with nothing to contrast it against.

tips: A comparison goal is unmet unless both things appear in the same sentence with a contrast word between them.

whyCorrect: The colon defines the blank: the elements "are joined together into a single cohesive unit." A word meaning linked to one another is "interconnected." The list of parts — terraces, canals, water temples — is there to show what is being joined, not to suggest anything about their quality or age.

whyWrong.B: "Outmoded" means out of date, which the passage's praise of the system's lasting significance contradicts.
whyWrong.C: "Optional" would mean the parts can be left out, the opposite of forming one cohesive unit.
whyWrong.D: "Informal" describes a lack of official structure, which says nothing about the parts being joined.

tips: When a colon restates the blank, translate the restatement into one word before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: The cause is "widespread admiration" of Edwards's portraits, and the blank names what that admiration earns him "as an artist." Admiration converts into standing and reputation, which is what "prestige" means. The phrase "as an artist" also signals that the blank is professional standing, not a personal quality.

whyWrong.A: "Sympathy" is compassion, which admiration for skilled work does not produce.
whyWrong.C: "Assistance" is practical help, and being admired is not the same as being helped.
whyWrong.D: "Tolerance" means being put up with, a far weaker response than widespread admiration.

commonMistakes: Picking any positive-sounding noun; the blank must be the specific thing that admiration confers.

whyCorrect: The clause after the colon explains the situation: "forest researchers regularly dispute one another's classifications." So what is in short supply among scientists is agreement, and "consensus" is the word for shared agreement. Note that "how little" makes the blank a thing there is a shortage of, which is why disputes follow.

whyWrong.A: "Interest" would mean scientists do not care about the categories, but they argue about them constantly, which shows plenty of interest.
whyWrong.B: "Deliberation" means careful discussion, and the disputes show there is a great deal of it.
whyWrong.C: "Vigilance" means watchfulness, which has no bearing on whether classifications agree.

tips: "How little ___ there is" plus evidence of disagreement points to a word meaning agreement.

whyCorrect: After the colon the sentence describes buyers who "hadn't previously wanted to purchase baseball cards" crowding into the market. That is demand being called into existence by the price rise, so the blank needs a verb meaning to draw out or bring about. "Eliciting" means bringing forth a response, which is what the rising price did to these new buyers.

whyWrong.A: "Capitalizing" does not take a direct object this way and would mean profiting from demand that already exists.
whyWrong.B: "Exploiting" also presupposes existing demand, but the passage specifies buyers who previously had no interest.
whyWrong.D: "Satisfying" demand means meeting it, which would leave demand unchanged rather than producing the surge described.

commonMistakes: Reading "counterintuitive" as a signal that demand fell; the colon shows demand rose.

whyCorrect: The colon gives the reason directly: over many years "a substantial number of participants will withdraw or fall out of contact." The blank names that phenomenon, and the term for participants gradually dropping out of a study is "attrition." Extra participants are recruited so that enough remain when some inevitably leave.

whyWrong.A: "Impartiality" is freedom from bias, which extra participants do not guarantee and which the colon does not describe.
whyWrong.B: "Replicability" is whether other researchers can repeat the study, not whether subjects stay in it.
whyWrong.D: "Circumspection" is caution, a quality of the researchers rather than a reason to enroll more people.

tips: The word after "because of" is defined by whatever follows the colon — here, people leaving over time.

whyCorrect: The first three sentences cover two tribal institutions — the Hibulb Cultural Center and the Turtle Mountain Band's center — both using traditional knowledge and addressing tribal citizens. The last sentence turns to museums that are not Indigenous-led and describes their different audience and design approach. That is two examples followed by a contrast with a third kind of institution.

whyWrong.A: No particular set of artifacts is described, and the non-Indigenous museums are contrasted in general rather than analyzed on the same objects.
whyWrong.B: Audience responses are never reported; the text describes who the exhibits are designed for, not how anyone reacted.
whyWrong.D: Both tribal centers use the same strategy, and nothing is presented as earlier or newer.

tips: Count how many things the passage discusses and in what order — that alone eliminates most structure choices.

whyCorrect: The first sentence supplies what Nixon is "most famous for" — the Watergate scandal — which is the common perception. The word "But" then introduces facts that do not fit it: recognition of tribal sovereignty and an early health care reform effort. The passage explicitly calls his legacy "complex," which is another way of saying the familiar view is too simple.

whyWrong.A: The passage opens with a scandal, not an achievement, and never says historians disregard his accomplishments.
whyWrong.C: Magruder and Woods are named as associates in one scandal, not as figures being ranked against Nixon.
whyWrong.D: The later facts do not argue against the Watergate account; they add to it, which is complication rather than counterevidence.

commonMistakes: Treating any "but" as a rebuttal — here the second half complicates the first rather than disputing it.

whyCorrect: Text 2 ends by claiming that better automated genre classification would benefit users. Text 1's central objection is upstream of that: it questions "whether categorizing music by genre is useful" at all, calling genre categories ambiguous, subjective, and simplistic, and citing research suggesting other concepts may capture musical relationships better. So its author would grant nothing about the benefit and instead challenge the value of genre itself.

whyWrong.A: Text 1 is skeptical about the enterprise; predicting substantial advances endorses it.
whyWrong.C: Relative difficulty across genres is Text 2's territory, and Text 1 makes no claim about which genres are easier to classify.
whyWrong.D: Listener enjoyment within a genre is never discussed in Text 1.

tips: When one text doubts a premise the other assumes, the response attacks the premise, not the results.

whyCorrect: The passage sets one group of critics against another: some fault the books for endings that "arbitrarily stop," while others say the volumes should be read as a single long work rather than as separate texts with conventional endings. Both positions are about how the novels are structured, and the passage takes no side. The main idea is therefore the disagreement itself.

whyWrong.A: The passage never calls Master and Commander especially intricate or ranks it among O'Brian's books.
whyWrong.C: The second group compares the series to other multivolume works as an analogy; they do not argue it should copy Galsworthy's form.
whyWrong.D: No critic in the passage praises the novels as entertaining despite flaws; the second group denies there is a flaw.

commonMistakes: Choosing a summary of just one side when the passage is built as a two-sided disagreement.

whyCorrect: The passage gives two halves of Villasana's practice — celebrating cultural icons such as Prince, and honoring ordinary people such as a girl on a sidewalk — and the last sentence ties them together: she sees both as ways of showing "the power and interconnectedness of all people." A main idea has to hold both halves and the unifying purpose, which is what choice C states.

whyWrong.A: The passage says both approaches serve power and connection together, so it does not weigh one against the other in a single work.
whyWrong.B: No chronology is given; nothing says she started with famous subjects and moved on.
whyWrong.D: Scholarly attention to her works is never mentioned.

tips: When a passage's final sentence unifies two examples, that sentence usually carries the main idea.

whyCorrect: The student's claim has two parts: innovation in irrigation, and a resulting gain in efficiency. Choice D supplies both — sprinkler systems were developed in response to water scarcity, and they cut the share of national water use going to irrigation, with the world figure of 70% showing how much lower the US 45% is. That drop is efficiency produced by a new design.

whyWrong.A: This compares humidity and the need for irrigation across regions, saying nothing about innovation or efficiency.
whyWrong.B: This argues that efficiency gains would be valuable, which is a case for pursuing them rather than evidence that they happened.
whyWrong.C: This shows a very old design still in use, which speaks to durability rather than to improvement over time.

commonMistakes: Accepting a quotation that mentions efficiency without checking whether it reports an actual increase.

whyCorrect: The critic's alternative rests on heart rate alone, since a slower heart rate can mean either relaxation or heightened attention. But the study also measured pupil size, which decreased during the lullaby. If attention normally makes pupils get larger, then the shrinking pupils point away from the attention explanation and the critic's account fails to fit the second measure.

whyWrong.A: Parents' preferences say nothing about what the infants experienced.
whyWrong.B: Unfamiliarity with the lullaby, if anything, makes the attention explanation more plausible rather than less.
whyWrong.C: Blinking was not measured in the study, so a fact about blinking cannot bear on these results.

tips: When a critic reinterprets one measurement, look for the second measurement in the passage — that is usually where the weakening evidence lives.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is comparative: a late first freeze helps invasive species more than native ones. Support therefore has to show both species gaining from the delay, with the invasive gaining more. Choice A does that — in late-freeze years both kept producing leaves longer, but the extension was much greater for the invasive P. aviculare than for the native V. edule, so the invader converted the extra warm days into more growing time.

whyWrong.B: If neither species changed its leaf production despite year-to-year swings in freeze timing, the delay confers no advantage on anyone.
whyWrong.C: Here the invasive stops producing leaves sooner in late-freeze years, which is the opposite of an advantage.
