whyWrong.D: An early spring in the same years introduces a second cause, so the extra leaves cannot be credited to the delayed freeze — and both species gained equally anyway.

commonMistakes: Accepting evidence that the invasive did well without checking that it did better than the native.

whyCorrect: The conventional view being tested is that valence — how pleasant a smell seems — is shaped by culture. The study drew on ten widely separated communities and found that people ranked the odors much the same way regardless of where they lived, with near-universal agreement that eugenol beats caprylic acid. Shared rankings across very different cultures is evidence against culture doing the shaping, so the results call the standard view into doubt.

whyWrong.A: The study measured whether culture shapes odor preference, not whether odor preference shapes culture; that reverses the direction being tested.
whyWrong.B: No comparison is reported between agreement on pleasant odors and agreement on unpleasant ones.
whyWrong.C: The conventional wisdom stated in the passage is about cultural mediation, not about whether pleasantness can be measured objectively.

tips: Identify the exact belief the study set out to evaluate; the completion has to speak to that belief and no other.

whyCorrect: The finding is split by species: small white herons prefer heavy canopy cover, little blue herons show no such preference. So a management strategy that adds tree canopy is working with one species' known preference and not the other's. The completion has to express that asymmetry — such a strategy is less likely to draw little blue herons than small white herons.

whyWrong.B: Lifespan was never studied; the research looked at how birds choose where to live.
whyWrong.C: Nothing suggests canopy makes the area less appealing to either heron, and no other species were examined.
whyWrong.D: Birds that do not live in wetlands are outside the study entirely.

commonMistakes: Reading "this was not true for little blue herons" as evidence that canopy repels them — it only means canopy does not attract them.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences: "the exhibition set out to provide a wide-ranging overview...through the 1950s" and "its efforts were largely successful." Joining two independent clauses takes a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, or a period. Choice C gives the comma and "and."

whyWrong.A: "And" without the comma is not enough to join two independent clauses.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.D: A lone comma between independent clauses is a comma splice.

tips: Cover the blank and read each half aloud — if both are sentences, a bare comma can never be the answer.

whyCorrect: The subject is compound: "a state's voting record and polling data," two things joined by "and," which makes it plural. The interrupter "not its population size" is set off by commas and does not change the subject's number. A plural subject takes "determine."

whyWrong.A: "Determines" is singular and agrees with neither part of the compound subject taken together.
whyWrong.B: "Has determined" is singular and also shifts to a completed past that clashes with the general present-tense claim.
whyWrong.C: "Determining" is a participle, leaving the sentence with no main verb.

commonMistakes: Letting the nearby singular "population size" set the verb; a phrase introduced by "not" is never the subject.

whyCorrect: "Compiled" is the main verb and "climate data from several sites" is its direct object. Nothing ever separates a verb from the object that completes it, so no punctuation belongs in the blank. Choice B leaves the sentence intact.

whyWrong.A: A comma between the verb and its object breaks a unit that must stay together.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and "climate data from several sites..." is not one.
whyWrong.D: A colon must follow a complete clause, but the sentence is not complete until the object arrives.

tips: The long list of researcher names makes a pause feel natural; punctuation follows grammar, not breathing.

whyCorrect: Two jobs again. "Respectively" belongs with the first clause, since it tells you which date goes with which painting, and it takes a comma before it. Then "such allegorical artwork was particularly popular from the 15th through the late 18th centuries" is a second independent clause, so the boundary needs a semicolon. Choice B does both.

whyWrong.A: This drops the comma before "respectively" and joins two independent clauses with only a comma.
whyWrong.C: The comma after "respectively" leaves a comma splice between two complete sentences.
whyWrong.D: This puts the semicolon before "respectively," attaching it to the wrong clause and stranding it at the head of the second sentence.

tips: Handle the interrupter and the clause boundary separately — most choices get one right and the other wrong.

whyCorrect: "For a person of letters" modifies "award" — it tells you what kind of award is being called the most prestigious — so nothing should separate the two. Once that phrase is attached, everything before the blank's end is a complete sentence, and what follows is the award's name. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces that identification.

whyWrong.A: The semicolon cuts "award" off from the phrase describing it and leaves a fragment on each side.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, but "the Nobel Prize in Literature" is only a noun phrase.
whyWrong.C: This puts the colon before the modifying phrase, so the clause introducing the name is incomplete.

tips: Attach modifying phrases to their noun first; then decide what punctuation the sentence boundary needs.

whyCorrect: The material after the blank — "revealing how the personal and political authority Haudenosaunee women had...influenced the first suffragists" — is a participial phrase, not a sentence. A participial phrase describing the main clause attaches with a comma. Choice C supplies it.

whyWrong.A: A period leaves "Revealing how..." as a fragment with no subject or main verb, and "Century" should not be capitalized.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon demands an independent clause on the right, and a participial phrase is not one.
whyWrong.D: With no comma, "revealing" reads as modifying "century," as though the century were doing the revealing.

commonMistakes: Treating any long stretch of words as a clause; check for a subject and a conjugated verb before reaching for a semicolon.

whyCorrect: The two sentences report different levels of standing on the same list. The panda and the crocodile merely made the top twenty, while the tiger was beaten by nothing at all — it sat at the very top. The transition has to mark that difference in rank, and "in contrast" does.

whyWrong.A: "For instance" would make the tiger an example of animals landing in the top twenty, but the point is that it outranked them.
whyWrong.C: "Hence" claims the tiger's first-place finish follows from the panda and crocodile's placement, which is not a causal relationship.
whyWrong.D: "Alternatively" offers a competing option, and no alternative is being proposed.

tips: When two sentences give rankings of different magnitude, the relation is contrast, not example.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank says Montaigne constantly questions his own perspective; the sentence after gives his motto, "What do I know?" The motto is a question about the limits of his own knowledge, so it matches that habit exactly. A transition marking a neat fit between a described trait and a piece of evidence is "fittingly."

whyWrong.A: "Nowadays" contrasts the present with the past, but the motto is Montaigne's own, not a modern development.
whyWrong.B: "Still" concedes something despite the previous point, and the motto agrees with the previous point.
whyWrong.C: "Conversely" signals the opposite case, but the motto exemplifies rather than reverses the description.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a contrast word because the motto is phrased as a doubting question — the doubt is the whole point of the previous sentence.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the sculpture sits outdoors, exposed to rain, snow, heat, and humidity — conditions that normally damage a work. The second says it stays in good condition anyway, because it is made of corrosion-resistant steel. Because the outcome runs against what the exposure would lead you to expect, the blank needs a concessive transition, and "that said" is one.

whyWrong.A: "As a result" would make good condition the consequence of exposure to weather, which reverses the logic.
whyWrong.C: "In addition" would treat surviving the weather as another item in the same list, missing the tension between the two facts.
whyWrong.D: "On the contrary" is used to reject a preceding statement as false, but the exposure to weather is true and remains true.

tips: "On the contrary" contradicts a claim; "that said" concedes one and adds a qualification — the second is what you want when both facts stand.
